slides.text: Outliers: errors, or the most interesting rows?
slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson seven: outliers. Are they errors, or the most interesting rows in your data?

slides.text: A value far from the rest of the data
slides.sub: One loan of 50 million in a column of 50 thousands
slides.say: An outlier is a value that sits far away from the rest of your data. Picture one loan of fifty million in a column where most loans are around fifty thousand.

slides.text:
Typos
Measurement errors
Real rare events
slides.say: Outliers usually come from one of three places. A typo, like an extra zero. A measurement or system error. Or a real, rare event that actually happened.

slides.sub: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the middle 50% of the data
slides.say: A common way to flag them is the IQR rule. The interquartile range is the spread of the middle half of your data. Values more than one and a half times that range below the first quartile, or above the third quartile, get flagged as possible outliers.

slides.text: Outliers pull the mean. The median barely moves.
slides.say: Why care? A single extreme value can drag the mean a long way, while the median barely moves. That's why one outlier can make an average misleading.

slides.text: Sometimes the outlier is the story
slides.sub: Unusual is a reason to look, not proof of fraud
slides.say: In fraud work, the unusual transaction is often exactly what you want to find. But be careful: unusual is a reason to investigate, not proof that something is wrong.

slides.sub: Fix errors · keep real values · write down what you did
slides.say: So the takeaway: never delete outliers automatically. Fix the errors, keep the real values, and write down what you decided.

summary: An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data, caused by a typo, a measurement error or a genuine rare event. The IQR rule flags values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR; investigate them before deciding to fix, keep or remove.
practice: Write down these 10 numbers: 12, 15, 14, 13, 16, 15, 14, 13, 15, 95. Find Q1, Q3 and the IQR, use the 1.5×IQR rule to check whether 95 is an outlier, then compare the mean and the median with and without it.
